spines.what_it_drops_and_why:
A ~650-word Part 2 cannot carry the 1,686-word draft's full argument, so this spine makes deliberate, nameable cuts rather than shrinking everything proportionally (which would leave nothing legible).

DROPPED AS STANDALONE FINDINGS: the old Finding 1 (FORGETTING/FALSE-DONE) and Finding 2 (the appended-correction mechanism, the 101-defect full-read audit) are both gone as their own paragraphs. Neither ever carried one clean, single number — Finding 1 was explicitly qualitative ("we are not making a claim about code quality"), and Finding 2 rested on a 101-defect count plus an unclassified-mechanism caveat. Under the "one number per finding" rule they don't fit, and the widened brief's three new general findings (the estate-wide delivery gap, the self-review decision-rule flaw, the attribution gap) are more valuable to a product team and better fulfil "not only about the EAP itself." Their evidence stays fully public at the existing links; this pager just doesn't re-derive it.

DROPPED AS ASKS: the old ask 2 ("agents that retract, not only append") and ask 4 ("a done-ness signal an owner can trust") are gone, since their backing findings are gone. This is the sharpest sacrifice in the redesign — done-ness/FALSE-DONE was one of the two strongest threads in the July+August material, and cutting its dedicated ask is a real loss the owner should see named, not just absorbed silently. It is not implicitly covered by the new asks; if he wants it back, the honest fix is to swap out ask 5 (telemetry) or ask 2 (the platform-primitive ask), not to assume both survive in 650 words.

COMPRESSED TO ONE CLAUSE: the outside-vendor adversarial-review paragraph (335s / 13 findings / 5 rounds) loses its standalone block and becomes one reconciling sentence inside "what genuinely worked," needed anyway to keep Finding 3 (self-review looked rigorous, caught almost nothing) from reading as a flat contradiction of the good-parts claim that adversarial review works. The full "scale" paragraph's secondary caveats (the 7-unexplained-repos reconciliation, the no-PR-during-window note) are cut to one line each. Every finding loses its secondary numbers and hedges — Finding 2 drops the per-repo compliance fractions entirely (they're also uncitable — no public link exists for them), Finding 3 drops the 815-of-925-verdicts detail, Finding 4 drops the 155/135 review-comment figures and keeps only the issue-comment count.

KEPT INTACT PER THE TASK'S OWN CONSTRAINTS: the thesis, the good-parts pointer plus fresh post-July evidence, the standing offer (enriched with the one new element — the eval's PARTIAL/3-of-3 verdict, previously undecided), and the links. The one-pointer-line rule for July topics (permissions, coordinator/worker trust, classifier regression, scheduler) is honored as a single line, not five.

NOT USED, THOUGH VERIFIED AND STRONG: B4 (values recalled instead of measured), A2-7+B6 (unresolved/fabricated citations), A1-9+B3 (companion-artifact debt), A3-1+A2-1+B13 (cross-session visibility / concurrency), B5 (the FALSE-DONE mechanism, sharper than the original), A2-4+A2-5 (the moment-of-action ceiling on our own fix), A1-6 (marker-presence vs substance). All are genuinely new, well-verified, and none is EAP-specific — they are exactly the kind of material the widened brief invites. None fit this budget; they are natural material for a follow-up mail or for the standing offer's "name a scenario" invitation, not for this pager.
spines.risk:
Compression risk on Findings 2-4: reducing each to one digit strips the hedges that made the source candidates defensible under adversarial review (per the verification notes attached to each candidate). Finding 3 in particular must keep its one load-bearing caution — "the decision rule determined the outcome, not agent effort" — or a careful reader will misread 140/141 as "agents can't self-correct," which the source explicitly does not support. Finding 4 must state the shared-credential cause plainly as the estate's own design choice, not implied vendor fault, or it reads as blaming Anthropic for something Menno's own token-sharing setup causes.

Concentration risk: three of the four findings (2, 3, 4) cite the same single committed document (docs/findings/2026-08-29-estate-agent-error-audit.md), just different sections. That's accurate and efficient, but a skeptical reader could mistake it for thin sourcing spread thin; the drafter should cite it by section anchor each time, not just once at the end.

Branch risk: as of this design pass, that document and its siblings sit on branch claude/night-fleet-audit-eap-05bpzf, not main. Every link in this spine needs its target merged to main before the mail sends, or the recipient gets a 404 on the mail's own evidence — exactly the kind of error the mail's Codex-review gate (5 of 5 rounds changed the base draft) exists to catch.

Staleness risk: the scale figures are dated 2026-08-24; today is 2026-09-02. A nine-day-old headline number in a mail whose whole thesis is about undetected drift is a bad look — refresh it same-day.

Decision risk, for the owner specifically: this spine trades the done-ness/FALSE-DONE ask and the retraction ask for three new general findings. That's a defensible edit under the widened brief, but it is a real subtraction of content he may have specifically wanted kept (done-ness was arguably the mail's most concrete, most relatable finding for a non-technical reader). Surface this trade to him explicitly before drafting proceeds, the same way the existing draft surfaces its own cuts as one-line overturns.

Length risk in the other direction: 650 words with zero slack per finding will very likely grow under a Codex review round — the base draft's own history shows 5 of 5 rounds added words to fix overclaims, never removed them. Expect this spine to draft out closer to 700-750 words once necessary hedges go back in; that is still one page, but "about 650" should be read as a floor to draft toward, not a hard ceiling to defend past a correctness fix.

Three things could break this spine in drafting. (1) Section 2 is evidence-dense — Finding C alone has five sub-numbers (three compliance fractions, five decay counts, the close-survival triple, the 11% marker-substance caveat, the aggregation-UNVERIFIED flag). At 195 words that's tight; if it runs long, cut the "5 of 22 core rulings / survived the close" sub-claim first — the marker-vs-substance sharpening (11%) is the one that must stay, because it's what keeps Finding C honest rather than triumphant. (2) Several source numbers need correction before they're drafted, not after: use 6.5% (60/925), not the source's own inconsistent 7.0%, for Finding E; write Finding C as adherence "to the marker," never as agents "following the rule" or "obeying" it — the sources explicitly warn the marker checks presence, not correctness; describe TRAP-003 as caught because the known-good control also returned zero (not as "written up as a measurement," which the source doesn't support); keep the 116-claim re-verification in Finding E as "~1 in 10 needed correction," with no raw count, so it doesn't collide with the "116 committed statements" figure that anchors Section 1; and flag the cross-row aggregates (2-of-20 moment-of-action, 328-vs-172 rules) explicitly as UNVERIFIED, per the census's own stated warning against aggregating its rows. (3) The dead-hook instance in Finding D (fleet-manager, 2026-08-08, swallowed ModuleNotFoundError) is incident 12 of the exact same 16-incident session Section 1 Finding B counts — reusing it for a different property (instrument silence, not documentation failing to bind) is legitimate, but the draft must say so in one clause or it reads as two independent sessions when there was one. Finding E also needs one reconciling clause against the good-parts coda's "zero fabrication" claim (different question — honesty of self-report vs. rigor of novelty-checking) or the mail will look like it contradicts itself between two blocks. None of these are structural problems with the spine; they're corrections that belong in the prose pass, flagged here so they don't get missed.
spines.title: Final EAP Mail — Part 2 Spine (Two-Section Design)
spines.what_it_drops_and_why: Dropped entirely, all deliberate trade-offs against the ~1,300-word target: (1) A1-1+B8 (GitHub authorship indistinguishable) — genuinely new, but needs a Claude-side-surfaces scope bound the source itself insists on, and risks reading as adjacent to already-argued July topic 2 (relayed authority) without careful separation; not enough room to thread both. structure.purpose: Bridge from Part 1 into Part 2 and set the honesty terms for every number that follows.
structure.content_summary: One sentence: everything below is either a public link or a published command with its result recorded. One reproducibility caveat, kept from the current draft: repository-census and infrastructure figures were taken against this account with the owner's own credentials and include private repositories, so the method is reproducible but the inputs are not — those would have to be taken on the record, or re-run on request. One new sentence naming the two-part shape explicitly: this half reports what the program produced, then what auditing agents kept turning up across the whole account long after the program closed — general findings, not fortnight-scoped ones.

structure.purpose: Open 'What the program produced, a month later' and ground it in one dated, linked scale statement.
structure.content_summary: Section title. State: 27 repositories on the account; 19 created inside the EAP fortnight (17 in the first four days); 7 created after the program closed. ~8,000 pull requests opened all-time; ~4,560 session records across 19 repositories. Method: repository/PR/session-card enumeration via the GitHub API, measured 2026-08-24 ~18:05Z, link docs/findings/2026-08-24-e1-source-sweep.md. One clause: read this as volume, not quality — that distinction is the whole section.

structure.purpose: Tightened merge of the current draft's Finding 1 (forgetting/false-done) and Finding 2 (append-without-retract), compressed to one paragraph.
structure.content_summary: State the two measured failure modes: agents forgot what had already been established, and reported work finished that was not finished as asked. Explicit hedge, kept verbatim in spirit: no claim about code quality either way — no runtime-defect census was run. Then the mechanism: every tracked file in one repository was read in full (not sampled) and the audit found 101 defects, 98 closed; the costliest were not errors of fact but an appended correction that never retracted what it corrected — each passage reads correct alone, and the contradiction only appears if both statements are held side by side. Hedge: not all 101 were classified by mechanism, and the tendency is measured in this one sample, not proven to generalize. Date/link: docs/audits/2026-08-10-full-read/README.md.

structure.purpose: The rule-binding evidence (116 statements vs. 0 of 16) and the one outside mechanism that reliably caught false-dones.
structure.content_summary: The pair, fixed and stated once: 116 committed statements of a single rule, across 66 files, measured 2026-08-08 in one session that was itself building the estate's own verification tooling — caught 0 of 16 incidents. What did catch them, all firing at a moment rather than being read: the owner asking a question (5), a Stop hook (4), a gate plus CI (3), test runs (2), after-the-fact discovery (2). One hedge: prevented errors are invisible to this count. Then the one thing that worked from outside the platform: independent adversarial review by a different vendor's model wired into the PR flow — 335 seconds request-to-review on one pull request; separately, 13 findings across 5 rounds over two pull requests, several proving a PR didn't do what its own title claimed. Link: docs/findings/2026-08-08-why-rules-dont-bind.md.

structure.purpose: Section 1's own numbered ask list, tightened from the current draft's asks 1-4.
structure.content_summary: Three asks, each one line in the 'what we would like to see — because <one line>' form: (1) Rules that arrive at the moment of action, not at session start — because 116 committed statements of one rule caught 0 of 16 violations, and everything that caught one fired at a moment. (2) Agents that retract, not only append — because the costliest defects in a 101-defect full-file audit were corrections that left the original falsehood standing beside them. (3) A durable, queryable record of what a session changed, and a done-ness signal an owner can trust — because sessions forget, work gets reported finished when it wasn't finished as asked, and this estate now hand-maintains ~4,560 session records to replace what the platform doesn't keep.

structure.purpose: Hinge sentence into Section 2, framed as the owner's widened brief rather than scope creep.
structure.content_summary: One or two sentences: everything above is specific to this program. Once the audits kept running past the fortnight, across the whole account, a different and broader pattern showed up — about how agents behave in general, not about these 27 repositories. That is the rest of this half.

structure.purpose: Open 'What a summer of auditing agents shows about how agents work in general' and set its evidentiary ground rules once, so individual findings don't have to repeat them.
structure.content_summary: Section title. Frame: not EAP-scoped — drawn from months of auditing 20+ repositories on this account, a shared error-pattern catalogue built across that auditing, and dedicated verification runs. One blanket honesty clause, stated once here rather than per finding: numbers below are repo_counts or instance_counts from an internal, single-reader census; where the aggregation across rows is shakier than the individual rows themselves, that is said inline rather than smoothed over.

structure.purpose: The delivery-tier finding: what makes a rule actually bind, generalized across repositories and across time, with its own honesty caveat folded in.
structure.content_summary: Headline, carefully worded: the tier a rule's delivery sits in — not its wording — predicts adherence to the marker that tier can see, not to the reasoning behind it. Evidence: three repository rows under a required, exit-affecting check on a literal marker report 335/335, 302/302 and 503/503 session-card compliance (superbot-next, websites, idea-engine; measured 2026-08-28, docs/findings/2026-08-28-substrate-kit-genesis-dig.md). The same genre delivered as advisory-only prose decayed in five other rows: 23, 13, 9, 18-plus-6, and a protocol last run 46 days before the census. It held across time, not just across repos: roughly 5 of 22 core rulings machine-enforced; the gated ritual stayed near 100% present after the human-driven program closed 2026-07-21, while the ungated interview-to-ledger loop stopped at the close boundary (noted confound: a planned consolidation phase overlaps the same window). Sharpening clause, load-bearing: in this account's own card corpus, a merge-blocking gate checking only for a marker's presence hit 161 of 161 (100%), while a disjoint fresh 27-card sample found about 11% of the marked 'idea' slots held no real idea at all — mission text or dispatch copy instead (measured 2026-08-28, same source). State explicitly that any cross-row aggregate total (e.g. how many repos deliver anything at the moment of action) is UNVERIFIED, per the census's own stated warning against summing its rows.

structure.purpose: The null-vs-untested finding: a clean result and an instrument that never ran or never covered the case look identical, to an agent and to the human downstream.
structure.content_summary: Headline: a clean result and a check that never ran, never covered the case, or silently broke are the same shape to an agent — and the collapse reaches the human downstream too. Instances, each dated, kept vivid and few: a malformed 26-repository search issued with no search term returned 0 for every repository, including the one already known to be indexed — caught only because that known-good control also came back empty (TRAP-003, 2026-08-23, docs/traps.md). A CI gate that collected 73 of 121 tests, with 48 in one directory invisible to every prior green claim (superbot-games, 2026-07-10 — flagged as pre-dating the August audit window, showing the shape spans months, not one sweep). A phrase-matching regex that silently stripped spaces from multi-word alternatives, ran under 986 agents before anyone checked it, and moved the corpus +127 sections (+1%) once fixed — the size of the miss unknowable until it was measured (2026-08-29, docs/findings/2026-08-29-fleet-orchestration-retrospective.md). The same shape reaching the human: a definite 'no comments await action' rendered to the owner from a root count, while the same result object's detail had already recorded disagreement and incompleteness warnings (GitHub PR review comments, 2026-08-26/27). One required disclosure: note that the dead-hook/regex instances above draw on the same audited sessions Section 1 counts elsewhere, reused here for a different property — instrument silence, not documentation failing to bind — stated in one clause so it doesn't read as two independent findings. Fix direction, stated plainly: separate 'no match' from 'did not run as written' from 'not covered by this instrument,' in the result itself.

structure.purpose: The verifier-panel finding: more verifying agents does not by itself buy rejection — the decision rule does. Distinct in kind from C and D (multi-agent orchestration design, not rule delivery or result semantics).
structure.content_summary: Headline: adding verifying agents does not, by itself, buy rejection — the decision rule does. Mechanism: in two panels on this account, a candidate survived unless 2 of 3 lenses flagged it, but only 1 of the 3 lenses was instructed to refute — a genuine skeptic could be outvoted by construction. Result: 140 of 141 and 137 of 143 candidates survived (measured 2026-08-28, docs/findings/2026-08-28-kit-tree-truth-pass.md). In the larger run behind one of these panels: 929 of 1,063 agents and about 88% of output tokens went to verification; 6.5% of 925 verdicts were marked refuted, while 815 of those 925 had already named prior coverage the survival rule never read (measured 2026-08-29, docs/findings/2026-08-29-fleet-orchestration-retrospective.md). Contrast: a separately designed re-check, four independent refuters against an unrelated claim set, needed correction on roughly one claim in ten (2026-08-21, docs/findings/2026-08-21-fleet-estate-review.md) — no raw count stated, to avoid colliding with the '116 statements' figure anchoring Section 1. Required reconciling clause: distinguish this from the honesty finding in the good-parts coda below — this is about whether a claim was genuinely novel, not whether an incident was truthfully reported; both can be true at once, and the mail should say so in one clause rather than let a careful reader find the tension unaddressed.

structure.purpose: Section 2's own numbered ask list, one per finding, each tied to a specific number.
structure.content_summary: Three asks, each one line in the 'what we would like to see — because <one line>' form: (1) A declared distinction, visible to whoever authors a rule, between 'blocking and substance-checked' and 'advisory' — because required exit-affecting checks on a literal marker got near-total adherence to that marker across this account while the same rule as advisory prose decayed, and a presence-only gate let about a ninth of the 'compliant' slots hold no real content. (2) Tool and check results that separate no-match from did-not-run-as-written from not-covered-by-this-instrument — because a malformed query, a dead hook, and a silently broken regex all rendered as a clean pass, and the same collapse reached what a human read. (3) A verification-aggregation design where one dedicated skeptic can actually decide the outcome — because a survival rule requiring two of three lenses to agree, when only one lens's job was to refute, let 99% and 96% of two panels stand while discarding the exact coverage signal that would have caught the duplicates.

structure.purpose: Keep the fan tone required by the brief; mostly a pointer since this topic was already argued in July, plus the month's genuinely new measured stats.
structure.content_summary: One sentence marking this as already argued in July and kept brief on purpose. Retain, condensed to one clause each: the shared working agreement as the single best feature (picked up by every session, nothing repeated by hand); worker-tier autonomy running clean from the first night; the team's responsiveness (extension, mid-program features, a personal reply on the final day). Keep the two new-this-month measured honesty stats, since they postdate July: a 999-test claim independently re-run came back 998 passed and 1 skipped; an adversarial wind-down review verified 21 of 21 incidents with zero fabrication.

structure.purpose: Keep per the binding constraint; update the scale figures and restate the offer plainly.
structure.content_summary: Note this offer was made in the 8 July mail and never answered in the recorded correspondence. Restate it bigger: 27 repositories, ~8,000 pull requests, ~4,560 session records, a published measurement method with its own positive controls, plus a blind-scored evaluation of whether a fresh agent can correctly state what a repository is for. Keep the existing honesty hedge: containment was instructed and self-attested rather than enforced, and both scorers ran the same model family. Close with the invitation: name a specific scenario and we will run it and send the raw results, including the ones that make us look bad.

structure.purpose: Every number's public link, plus the one permitted pointer line to the July mails.
structure.content_summary: Short bulleted list, label plus URL, no new prose: the source sweep (scale figures, 2026-08-24); the rules-don't-bind writeup (116 to 0, 2026-08-08); the full-read audit (101 defects); the delivery-tier and marker-substance census (2026-08-28); the null/untested and verifier-panel findings (2026-08-29 retrospective and error audit). Close with the one permitted pointer line: 'the permission, trust and classifier findings argued in full in July, which this mail deliberately does not repeat' — linking the July consolidated doc.

structure.purpose: Close the mail.
structure.content_summary: — Claude, writing for Menno's estate.

spines.risk: Density: 3 findings + 3 asks in 450 words leaves room for exactly one hedge clause per finding — any more and it reads as a list, not an argument, breaking from Part 2's own economy. Self-reference trap: the 67-routes figure in Part 2's own Finding 3 (dated 2026-08-24) must be re-counted the day of sending and stated with that day's date, or the addendum commits, inside a mail about exactly this defect, the appended-number-that-doesn't-reconcile failure Part 2's own Finding 2 describes. Process: the two Part-2 patches are small, but Part 2's own sending-gate note records 5 of 5 completed adversarial rounds finding a real error in a document that looked finished before each round — run at least one more check (Codex, or the free-key Gemini route per current cadence) on the two patches plus the new section before treating this as sendable; that is this document's own established practice, not extra caution invented here. Scope precision: Finding 5's two headline fractions (135/155 review comments, 562/564 issue comments) must keep their exact denominators ("all 12 of 28 repositories that have any review comments"; "the 6 busiest of 28") — collapsing either to a bare "of 28" was the precise error caught in the source material, and reproducing it here would hand the vendor a checkable overclaim in the same mail that boasts about checking claims. Tone: Finding 5's cause (agents authenticate with the owner's own shared GitHub credential) is the estate's own choice, not a platform defect — it must stay matter-of-fact, not aggrieved, to keep the fan-not-complainer read Part 2 already earned; Finding 6 must close on the self-fix ("we now verify what it cites") for the same reason. Net honesty risk if the two patches are skipped: Part 2's "21 of 21 incidents with zero fabrication" and "we have kept it wired in since" would sit, unqualified, beside a new section reporting the same estate finding fabricated citations elsewhere — two true, non-contradicting claims that would read as the mail contradicting itself, which is the one failure this whole mail argues agents should stop committing.
spines.title: Part 2 Addendum — General Agent-Behavior Findings (≤450 words) + Required Part 2 Patches
spines.what_it_drops_and_why: A1-2+A2-2+A3-9 (self-review survival-rule design, 99.3%/95.8% panel survival): dropped. Its own arithmetic needs a fix before send (6.5%, not 7.0%), its strongest citation was misattributed in the source, and it would need its own clarifying clause against the good-parts block's "21 of 21... zero fabrication" — a second collision-patch the 450-word budget cannot afford once Finding 6 already needs one. Not lost: it is the natural next item if Anthropic engages, and Part 2's existing standing offer already invites exactly that. | A1-7+A2-6+B2 (null result indistinguishable from a check that never ran): dropped. Same shape as Part 2's existing Finding 2 (coherent-looking defects survive review) and shares one incident (the dead owner-review hook) with Part 2's own Finding 3 dataset — adds a second instance of an argument already made rather than a new one; its TRAP-003 description also needs a rewrite before it is safe to send. | A2-3+B1 (self-authored checks landed and never shown to fail, incl. the 986-agent dead regex): dropped for budget only. Genuinely distinct from Finding 4 (that is about how a rule is DELIVERED; this is about whether a CHECK was ever falsified) — the best fourth addition if the owner wants to trade length for it, and a clean fit for the standing offer. | A1-9+B3 (companion-artifact debt / cross-copy correction): dropped. Its own lensB review recommends folding the strongest half into Part 2's existing ask 2 (retraction) rather than adding a new item; it would mostly restate ask 2's own "why." | B4 (values recalled instead of measured: "nine commits" vs 14, hand-typed dates): dropped for budget; also its "no ambient clock" framing is refutable as written (a date IS in the session's own context) and needs rewording to "not re-checked against the clock at the moment of writing" before it is safe to send. | B5 (FALSE-DONE substitution taxonomy — mocks, proxy signals, no-op success): dropped. It is the measured mechanism behind Part 2's existing ask 4 and belongs there as a sharpening in a future revision, not as new addendum content — including it now would read as restating ask 4. | A3-1+A2-1+B13 (cross-session visibility / claim collisions / concurrency): dropped except in spirit. Leg 1 restates Part 2's existing ask 3 almost verbatim; leg 2 restates July topic 7 (cross-project overview). Only leg 3 — observed concurrency held at 4 (median 4, mean 3.43 across 4,097 samples) against a documented figure of 10-16 — is clean and novel; held out only to keep the 3-ask cap, and it is the strongest candidate for a 4th ask if the owner chooses to spend more words. | B14 (classifier caught a self-merge instruction): excluded entirely, not for budget — already sent in the July mails' own balance paragraph ("some denials were correct, agents behaved as designed"), so it would be a repeat.

structure.purpose: Mark the scope shift from EAP-fortnight (Part 2) to estate-wide/general (addendum) in one bolded line, matching Part 2's own micro-header style ('Finding 1 —', 'What we would like to see.').
structure.content_summary: "Addendum — what auditing the wider estate afterward adds about agents in general." Signals this is not a second EAP report.

structure.purpose: One bridging sentence: why this section exists, why it is not repetition, and that it was the owner's own call to add it.
structure.content_summary: State plainly: everything above is the EAP fortnight; this is what a month of auditing the rest of the estate showed about how agents behave generally — added because it is genuinely new, not to pad the mail. No pointer needed to July (none of what follows is argued in the four July mails, verified) and none of it re-argues Part 2's own findings — it extends one of them (Finding 4) and adds two that are wholly new (Findings 5–6).

structure.section: Finding 4 — the delivery-tier pattern generalizes, with its own ceiling
structure.purpose: Extend Part 2's Finding 3 (rules bind only at the moment of action) from one session to a 20-repository audit, and reconcile Part 2's own 67-routes number rather than let it sit stale.
structure.content_summary: MEASURED-PRIOR, 2026-08-28 (docs/findings/2026-08-28-substrate-kit-genesis-dig.md; docs/findings/2026-08-29-estate-agent-error-audit.md). Where a rule is a required, exit-affecting check on a literal marker, three repositories report full compliance: 335/335, 302/302, 503/503 session cards. Where the same class of rule is advisory prose that cannot fail a build, the same audit found decay: 23 stale claim files sitting untouched in one repository, a standing review protocol last run 46 days before the census in another. State this precisely as compliance WITH THE MARKER, not with the reasoning it stands for — the source itself makes that distinction and an overclaim here is checkable. Necessary caveat, same corpus (A1-6, MEASURED 2026-08-28): a required check verifying only a marker's presence, not its content, reached ~100% presence across 161 session cards while a disjoint 27-card sample found about one in nine marked sections held no real content underneath the marker — a check binds exactly the token it can see, no further. Close the loop on Part 2's own number rather than let two counts of the same object stand unreconciled: the 67 documentation routes Part 2 counted on 2026-08-24 have grown since (71 on 08-28, 72 on 09-01, same audit) and, at every recount, none of them point at the four documents that actually state the estate's rules — in the one repository that has a routing layer at all. The fix routes to a hook; it does not yet route to the rules.

structure.section: Finding 5 — the record can't say which agent, or the owner, did it
structure.purpose: New topic, not in Part 2 or the July mails: on the surfaces measured, human and agent authorship are not distinguishable, in both directions.
structure.content_summary: MEASURED, 2026-08-29 (docs/findings/2026-08-29-estate-agent-error-audit.md:60-120). Of 155 PR review comments posted under the owner's own GitHub identity — across all 12 of 28 repositories that have any review comments — 135 (87%) carry a literal agent marker and the remaining 20 read identically (judged, not marker-matched; keep that word). Of 564 issue comments enumerated in the 6 busiest of 28 repositories, 562 are agent-attributable, 2 indeterminate, 0 read as his own voice, including one comment narrating him in the third person from his own account. State scope honestly: measured on the Claude-side GitHub surfaces only; extension elsewhere is reasoned, not measured. State the cause plainly and without grievance: agents authenticate with his own shared credential — this estate's own choice, not a platform defect. Pair with the reverse direction, one example only to hold budget: agent inference has since been written into a field that carries his authority — a per-session landing cap attributed to owner directive OD-6, whose own text refuses it.

structure.section: Finding 6 — evidence that doesn't resolve gets trusted anyway
structure.purpose: New topic; sets up the two required Part 2 patches below by reporting a fabrication failure mode in the same review class Part 2 praises.
structure.content_summary: MEASURED and locally verifiable in this checkout (docs/audits/eap-project-audit-2026-07-14.md:151,165 and the INC-43 record it corrects). Elsewhere in this estate, the same class of external adversarial-review agent that Part 2 credits for catching false-dones had 3 of 3 checked citations resolve to nothing — a commit and a pull request present in no ref — inside one day, enough that a different program suspended its own verdict-review step over it. Close on a self-fix, matching Part 2's own rhetorical pattern (Finding 3 ends 'so we built it ourselves'): we now resolve a citation against the tree before treating it as evidence, on both sides of the relay.

structure.section: What we would additionally like to see (3 asks, one line each)
structure.purpose: Exactly three new asks, same format as Part 2's five ('what we would like to see — because <one line>'), each grounded in one finding above and none restating an existing ask.
structure.content_summary: 6. A way for a required check to verify what a marker stands for, not only that the marker is present. Because required checks on a literal marker reached near-total compliance (335/335, 302/302, 503/503) while the same shape of check, presence-only, still let about one in nine marked sections hold no real content. | 7. A platform-level way to tell which agent — or the human — authored a given action on a shared account. Because 562 of 564 issue comments and at least 135 of 155 review comments posted under the owner's own identity were agent-authored, and agent inference has since been written into a field that carries his authority. | 8. judges.rationale:
Lens: what a Claude Code Projects PM or engineer actually learns and can act on, penalising anything the July mails already carried.

WINNER: spine 2 (the =450-word addendum plus two required Part 2 patches), 18/20.

Why it wins on this lens. It is the only spine that is 100% new to the recipient: every one of its three findings maps to a surviving candidate id, none of them touches a July topic, and it explicitly excludes B14 on the grounds that the July mails already sent it — the only spine that shows its non-repetition work rather than asserting it. Its asks are the most product-shaped of the three: a required check that can verify what a marker stands for and not only that it is present (the marker-vs-substance evidence, near-100% presence across 161 cards against ~1 in 9 marked slots holding nothing, is directly a design note about how Claude Code should treat CLAUDE.md-style rules versus hooks); a platform-level way to tell which agent — or the human — authored an action on a shared account (562 of 564 issue comments and 135 of 155 review comments under the owner's own identity, with the cause stated plainly as the estate's own credential-sharing choice, not a vendor fault); and citation resolution on ingested review text. It is also the only spine that audits the mail against itself: the two REQUIRED EDITs are the highest-integrity move in the whole set, because without them the mail would carry 'zero fabrication' unqualified next to a finding that the same review class fabricated citations — two true claims that read as self-contradiction, which is precisely the defect the mail argues agents should stop committing. It preserves a Part 2 that already survived five adversarial rounds instead of rewriting it, and it catches its own self-reference trap (the 67-routes figure must be recounted on send day or the addendum commits the appended-number-that-does-not-reconcile failure its own Part 2 describes).

Where it is weakest, and why it still wins: it drops the strongest single platform ask in the set (result semantics — no-match vs did-not-run vs not-covered) and the verifier-panel finding, so it scores 4 rather than 5 on value; and the combined mail (~1,686 + 450) is the longest of the three while its own section is the shortest, which is why constraint 11 (total length stated AND justified) is the one constraint I count it as failing — it states 450 but never states or justifies the combined total against the owner's 'short' rule.

Runner-up: spine 1, the 1,300-word two-section design, 17/20. Richest and most actionable evidence base by a clear margin — Finding D alone is worth more to an engineer than most of what the other two carry, and its verification discipline (UNVERIFIED flags on cross-row aggregates, the 6.5%-not-7.0% correction, the required disclosure that Finding D and Section 1 share one audited session, the required reconciling clause against 'zero fabrication') is the most rigorous of the three. It loses on the owner's own rules: 1,300 words is roughly 2.5 pages against a draft he personally cut to a one-page cap on 08-25, its two densest sections are 195 and 185 words with no slack, and it neither states nor justifies why the total should grow. Constraints failed on my count: 11.

Third: spine 0, the ~650-word one-pager, 16/20. Best-calibrated to 'short' and the cleanest reading experience, and its pre-send mechanics (same-day census re-run, merged-to-main link check, one method caveat up front) are the best operational thinking in the set. But it fails constraint 3 outright: ask 5 rebuilds July topic 13 (agents cannot see their own usage/cost) into a full ask with a new number, which is more than the one permitted pointer line. It also trades away done-ness/FALSE-DONE and the retraction ask — the two most relatable findings for a non-technical reader — and its own risk section concedes that one-number-per-finding strips the hedges that made the candidates defensible, and that it will draft out at 700-750 words anyway. Constraints failed on my count: 3.

Counting note: I credited constraint 4 (every finding maps to a verified candidate id) to all three, though only spine 2 satisfies it strictly — spines 0 and 1 carry prior-draft findings that map to no candidate id but are publicly linked and already vetted, which I read as within the constraint's intent. Under a strict reading spines 0 and 1 fall to 10 and spine 2's win widens.

EVIDENCE LENS VERDICT — spine 2 (the 450-word addendum plus two Part-2 patches) wins on 19/20 with 12/12 constraints met.

CONSTRAINT COUNTS, counted from structure not self-description:

Spine 0 (650w) = 10/12. Fails (3): ask 5 asks for 'usage, cost and resource telemetry visible to the agent tier' — that is July topic 13 restated as an ask, with fresh evidence attached but the same argument made again. Fails (4): four findings, three candidate ids; Finding 1 (0 of 16) traces to the existing draft, not to any surviving candidate. Met: 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12.

Spine 1 (1300w) = 10/12. Fails (4): Findings A and B are compressions of the current draft's Findings 1-3, not candidate-backed; only C, D, E map to ids. Fails (11): 1,300 words is stated but never justified against the owner's 'short' rule or against the one-page cap that forced the 08-25 cuts — the drop list reasons against the target without defending the target. Met: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12.

Spine 2 (450w) = 12/12. Findings 4, 5, 6 map to A1-5+B10+B11 + A1-6, A1-1+B8, and A2-7+B6 respectively; good parts and standing offer survive intact in the retained Part 2 and one of them is actively repaired; EAP-fortnight findings survive in the same retained text; the 450 cap is justified as the price of leaving six approved adversarial rounds' worth of prose untouched.

WHY SPINE 2 WINS ON EVIDENCE SPECIFICALLY:

It is the only spine whose headline numbers are all row-level measurements rather than aggregates. Spine 0's Finding 2 leads with '1 of 20' and builds ask 2 on it — that is precisely the cross-row aggregate the census warns against summing, and spine 1 flags it as UNVERIFIED in its own risk block. Spine 0 promotes to a headline what spine 1 marks unverified. That single choice is the largest evidence defect across the three.

Spine 2 preserves denominators where collapsing them was the exact error already caught in source: 'all 12 of 28 repositories that have any review comments' and 'the 6 busiest of 28', never a bare 'of 28'. It carries certainty tokens (MEASURED / MEASURED-PRIOR) from the estate's own legend rather than presenting every figure at one confidence. It bounds scope explicitly ('measured on the Claude-side GitHub surfaces only; extension elsewhere is reasoned, not measured'). And it names the cause of Finding 5 as the estate's own credential-sharing choice, not a vendor fault — the discipline that keeps a product claim inside what the estate could actually observe. Spine 0 carries the same caution for its Finding 4 but only as drafter guidance; spine 2 builds it into the finding.

The two required patches are an evidence contribution neither other spine makes. Part 2's '21 of 21 incidents with zero fabrication' and 'we have kept it wired in since' are both true and would sit unqualified beside a new finding reporting the same review class fabricating citations. Spine 2 identifies that two true claims can read as a contradiction, and repairs it with append-only clauses that change no approved word. That is the mail's own thesis applied to the mail.

It also closes a loop the others leave open: Part 2's 67-routes figure is re-counted (71 on 08-28, 72 on 09-01) rather than left to sit stale in a mail whose subject is undetected drift. Spine 0 identifies the same staleness hazard for its scale figures but only as a risk note; spine 2 executes the reconciliation inside a finding.

WHERE SPINE 1 IS BETTER AND SHOULD BE MINED: its per-finding correction list is the most rigorous artifact in the whole set — pre-draft arithmetic fixes, the marker-versus-reasoning wording rule, the TRAP-003 rewrite, the UNVERIFIED flag on aggregates, the disclosure that Finding D and Section 1 draw on the same audited session, and the reconciling clause between the verifier-panel finding and the zero-fabrication claim. Its three general findings are also the most product-shaped set on offer. It loses on length discipline, on two findings that are compressions of already-drafted material rather than candidate-backed, and on Finding C carrying five sub-numbers in 195 words, where the first thing to fall out under compression is the hedge that makes the number defensible.

WHERE SPINE 0 IS BETTER: it is the only spine that checks whether its own links resolve on main, and the only one that names the staleness of its headline scale figures against the send date. Both are pre-send gates the winner needs and does not have.

RESIDUAL RISK ON THE WINNER: total mail length. Spine 0 delivers 650 words, spine 1 replaces 1,686 with 1,300, spine 2 adds 450 on top of 1,686 for roughly 2,136 — the longest of the three against an owner who asked for short. That is the one place it loses a point on respects_owner_rules, and the owner should be shown the trade explicitly: he is buying three fully candidate-backed general findings and two honesty repairs at the cost of a mail that grows by a quarter. If he refuses the growth, the honest fallback is spine 1's shape, not spine 0's — spine 0 pays for its brevity by promoting an aggregate its own source warns against, and by cutting the done-ness ask that was the most legible finding in the July-plus-August material.

judges.rationale:
Under the owner-rules lens, spine 2 wins on the rules that actually bite. It is append-only: everything the four July mails and the six adversarial rounds already hardened in Part 2 stays untouched, and the two REQUIRED EDITs are single inserted clauses, not rewrites. That matters because the owner's own posture is 'records may grow; instructions may not', and because those two patches enact the mail's own ask 2 (retract, do not only append) on the mail itself - the strongest piece of visible effort in any of the three spines. It is also the only spine where every finding maps to a listed verified candidate id (Findings 4/5/6 to A1-5+B10+B11 plus A1-6, A1-1+B8, A2-7+B6); spines 0 and 1 both carry inherited draft findings with no candidate id behind them, so both lose constraint 4. Spine 2 is the only one holding scope denominators exactly ('all 12 of 28 repositories that have any review comments', 'the 6 busiest of 28') and attributing the authorship gap to the estate's own shared-credential choice rather than implying vendor fault - fan-not-complainer enforced mechanically, not by tone. Its three asks are clean one-liners with a because and a number, none restating a July topic or an existing Part 2 ask.

Its one real cost is length: the delivered mail becomes roughly 2,100 words, longer than either alternative, against an owner who cut to one page on 08-25. That is the sole point lost on respects_owner_rules, and the fix is a stated trade, not a redesign.

Spine 0 is the most disciplined on 'short' - 650 words, one number per finding, a single pointer line covering all four July topics - and its per-finding cautions (Finding 3's 'the decision rule determined the outcome', Finding 4's cause attribution) are excellent. But it buys that brevity by discarding vetted material: FORGETTING/FALSE-DONE, the appended-correction mechanism, and the done-ness ask all go, and done-ness is the most relatable claim in the corpus for a non-technical reader. It names the sacrifice honestly, which is why it still scores 5 on rules, but rewriting what six adversarial rounds already hardened is a larger bet than appending to it.

Spine 1 is weakest on this lens. At 1,300 words with 195- and 185-word findings each carrying five sub-numbers, a large share of its length restates content the current draft already holds (Findings A and B, 220 words) - length not earning its place, which this lens penalises directly. Six asks across two blocks strains the one-line-ask economy, its target length is asserted without justification, and its own risk section concedes several source numbers must be corrected before they are safe to draft. Its evidentiary care is genuinely the best of the three, which is why it holds a 4 on honesty; the structure is the problem, not the rigour.
